paper_title: Do Underwater Image Quality Metrics Agree with Human Perception? A Benchmark with Human Choices, Simple Edits and Generative Drift

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Underwater image enhancement is challenging to evaluate due to the lack of clean reference images, so researchers rely on no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics. However, it remains unclear whether these metrics agree with human judgments. We evaluate 73 handcrafted underwater, learned underwater, vision-language and general-purpose metrics against human preferences on five references: four published opinion-score sets and a new paired-comparison study. For each metric, we measure how often it selects the same image as people when comparing versions of the same scene. We further test whether simple image edits and small adversarial perturbations raise metric scores above the enhancement people preferred, and whether scores decrease as repeated generative edits add noise. Our results show that no metric consistently matches human preferences. The best worst-case Cohen's kappa over the five references is only 0.23 (Q-Align), while two raters in our study agree with a median kappa of 0.41. The widely used UCIQE often favors edits that people reject. On a Nano Banana Pro replica chain that should leave the image unchanged, only 22 of 73 scores decrease at every checkpoint, while noise grows by 2.5 times. We also introduce TrustUIQA, a benchmark that combines the human references, our study choices, the edited, attacked and generated images, and the scores of every metric on every image. The code is available at https://github.com/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA and TrustUIQA at https://huggingface.co/datasets/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA.

However, it remains unclear whether these metrics agree with human judgments. We evaluate 73 handcrafted underwater, learned underwater, vision-language and general-purpose metrics against human preferences on five references: four published opinion-score sets and new paired-comparison study. For each metric, we measure how often it selects the same image as people when comparing versions of the same scene. We further test whether simple image edits and small adversarial perturbations raise metric scores above the enhancement people preferred, and whether scores decrease as repeated generative edits add noise. Our results show that no metric consistently matches human preferences. The best worstcase Cohens κ over the five references is only 0.23 (QAlign), while two raters in our study agree with median κ of 0.41. The widely used UCIQE often favors edits that people reject. On Nano Banana Pro replica chain that should leave the image unchanged, only 22 of 73 scores decrease at every checkpoint, while noise grows by 2.5. We also introduce TrustUIQA, benchmark that combines the human references, our study choices, the edited, attacked and generated images, and the scores of every metric on every image. The code is available at https: //github.com/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA and TrustUIQA at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA. 1. Introduction Underwater images lose red light, contrast and detail with depth, and many enhancement methods aim to restore them. Since no clean reference exists for real underwater image, these methods are compared using no-reference image quality assessment (NR-IQA) metrics. UIQM [41] and UCIQE [58] are the most common choices, learned metrics trained on underwater opinion scores are increasingly used [18, 23, 61], and general vision-language models such as Q-Align [55] can also score underwater images. In each case, higher score is interpreted as better image. The same assumption underlies other restoration tasks, where general NR-IQA metrics such as NIQE [38] rank low-light enhancement [25] and perceptual super-resolution [5] methods. This interpretation holds only if the metric orders images as people do, and Fig. 1 shows cases where it does not. In all three photos, UCIQE assigns its highest score to the S+S+C edit applied 20 times or to the 50th Pro replica frame, and URanker [18] and MANIQA [60] score the 20-times edit above the reference, whereas NR-UIQA [61] ranks the reference first. Since few examples are not conclusive, this paper measures how often such reversals occur. We evaluate 73 metrics (7 hand-crafted underwater, 7 learned underwater, 2 vision-language and 57 general-purpose) against five human references and address four questions. (1) Do metrics choose between enhancements of the same photo as people do? (2) Do learned underwater metrics generalize to data from other labs? (3) Can simple edits or small gradient steps raise score above the enhancement people preferred? (4) Do metrics detect the noise and color shifts introduced by repeated generative edits? Our results show that the answer to (1) and (2) is mostly no and the answer to (3) is yes. For (4), most scores miss these changes under the strict rule of Banana100 [49], and some, including UCIQE, even rise. Our main contributions are as follows: within-scene agreement evaluation of 73 metrics on five human references (Secs. 3 and 4): four published opinion-score sets (12,360 images, 1,160 scenes) and new paired-comparison study with 20 raters and 1,920 choices. The best worst-case κ is only 0.23 (Q-Align). The five learned underwater metrics with known training set reach 0.60 to 0.92 on it, but at most 0.31 on data from other labs. Noise increases by 1.4 to 2.8. On the Pro replica chain, where the image should not change, only 22 of 73 scores decrease at every checkpoint and 38 by the last step, while UCIQE increases on every chain. In addition, Sec. 7 shows that the public UCIQE code returns no score for 27% to 38% of the opinion-score images and offers hypothesis for why its formula rewards simple edits. Section 8 summarizes the results as five recommendations for future evaluations. 2. Related work Underwater quality metrics and opinion-score sets. Hand-crafted underwater metrics combine color, sharpness and contrast measures: UIQM [41], UCIQE [58], CCF [52] and FDUM [59]. Learned metrics are trained on opinion scores of enhanced underwater images: URanker [18], NUIQ [23], Twice-Mixing [14], NMFC [10], NR-UIQA [61], UIQAVSI [11] and QUIQ [27]. The opinion-score sets they use, UID2021 [20], SAUD [23], SAUD2.0 [24] and SOTA [54], evaluate metrics by wholeset correlation with their scores. Other benchmarks avoid opinion scores by using color charts [4] or detection task [33]. Li and Cavallaro [30] found that UIQM, UCIQE

sections.content: 60 100 200 800 32 16 10 12 10 960 1,000 2,400 8,000 12 edits 1,920 choices Table 1. Five human references. The four opinion-score sets rate several enhancements of each underwater photo (a scene). Our study pairs raw UIEB [29] photo with one edit of it. and CCF do not match perceived quality, Lin et al. [32] reached similar conclusion from crowdsourced study of enhanced underwater images, and recent studies review and compare subjective and objective evaluation of underwater enhancement [40, 45]. We do not claim the first evidence of these limitations. Our contribution is the combination of five human references, including new study of simple edits, with 73 metrics, simple-edit baselines, stress tests and implementation checks. Testing quality metrics. gMAD [35] compares metrics on images where they disagree most, and later work identifies failures of blind models in the wild [53]. BAPPS [64] evaluates metrics by how often they match two-alternative human choice, and Q-Bench [56] tests the low-level perception of vision-language models. Optimizing images for quality model can raise its score without improving the images [13], small gradient attacks raise many NR-IQA scores [3, 67], and defenses against such attacks have been benchmarked [19]. Unlike these general studies, we test underwater images and metrics, add simple image edits as gradient-free way to manipulate scores, and compare edits and attacks with the enhancement people preferred in underwater opinion-score sets. Generative drift. Banana100 [49] asks Nano Banana Pro to copy an image 100 times and finds that many NR-IQA metrics do not decrease as the copies degrade. An evaluation on 14 low-level tasks finds its outputs visually good but behind on reference-based metrics [72]. Unlike Banana100, we run the test on underwater images with two editors and two prompts, an exact-copy prompt and an enhancement prompt, and include the hand-crafted and learned underwater metrics and RALI [69]. 3. Benchmark 3.1. Human references Table 1 lists the references. UID2021 [20], SAUD [23], SAUD2.0 [24] and SOTA [54] assign mean opinion score to every enhancement of every scene. SAUD and SAUD2.0 come from the same lab and share 33 photos, so we treat them as one group when evaluating generalization. Scene counts are per set, so these photos are counted twice in the 1,160 scenes. Our paired study. The opinion-score sets contain only outputs of published enhancement methods. To test edits that metric may reward but people may not, we conducted two-alternative forced-choice study on 32 raw UIEB [29] photos. Each trial shows the raw photo and one edited version side by side in random order with the question Pick the one with better overall quality. The 12 edits range from mild CLAHE [71], contrast, sharpening and saturation to strong noise and chain of the saturate, sharpen and CLAHE filters applied 5 or 20 times (Sec. of the appendix lists all strengths). Each rater saw one of four blocks of 8 photos, with 96 test trials plus 6 attention checks (a strongly blurred copy), 5 repeated pairs and 4 identical pairs. All 20 raters passed every attention check, which gives 160 votes per edit and 1,920 choices in total. Raters who saw the same block agree with median Cohens κ of 0.41 (range 0.11 to 0.54 over 55 pairs). We use this value as reference level for metric agreement, not as an upper bound. Of the 55 rater pairs, 36 come from the block with 9 raters. 3.2. Metrics We evaluate 73 metrics in four groups. Hand-crafted underwater (7): UIQM and its three terms UICM, UISM and UIConM [41], UCIQE [58], CCF [52] and FDUM [59]. Learned underwater (7): the seven metrics of Sec. 2, using the authors code and weights. NUIQ [23], NR-UIQA [61], UIQAVSI [11] and NMFC [10] were trained on SAUD, and QUIQ [27] on UID2021. URanker was trained on enhancements of all 890 UIEB raw photos [18], which include the photos of our study and drift test. Visionlanguage (2): Q-Align [55] and VisualQuality-R1 [57]. VisualQuality-R1 uses the prompt from its model card with greedy decoding. Every answer contained score, although 4% of the scores on the opinion-score sets fall below the nominal range of 1 to 5. General-purpose (57): the noreference metrics in IQA-PyTorch [7], several with more than one checkpoint, namely BRISQUE [37], NIQE [38], IL-NIQE [63], PIQE [50], NRQM [34], PI [5], CNNIQA [26], WaDIQaM [6], DBCNN [65], HyperIQA [47], MetaIQA [70], NIMA [48], PaQ-2-PiQ [62], MUSIQ [28], UNIQUE [66], TReS [15], MANIQA [60], CLIP-IQA [51], LIQE [68], TOPIQ [8], ARNIQA [2], QualiCLIP [1], the no-reference branch of A-FINE [9], MA-CLIP [31], the LAION aesthetic predictor [43, 44] and image entropy, plus RALI [69]. LIQE-mix was scored only on UID2021, SAUD and SAUD2.0. All scores are oriented so that higher is better, and lower-is-better scores such as NIQE are negated. Some of the 73 metrics are additional checkpoints of the same model (eight for ARNIQA) or terms of UIQM, so the metric counts below give these models more weight. UIQM follows the widely used FUnIE-GAN [22] code with two fixes (the trimmed-mean index and the UISM blue weight), FDUM is Python port of the authors MATLAB code, and CCF is our implementation of the published formula. UCIQE uses our NumPy port, which divides and chroma by 100 and takes the 1st to 99th percentile range of as contrast. Section 7 compares it with the public MATLAB code. 3.3. Agreement within scene An enhancement paper asks which of several outputs for the same photo is best. We therefore compare each metric with people on pairs of enhancements of the same scene. For each pair with different opinion scores, we check whether the metric prefers the same image as people, pool all pairs of set into one 2 2 table and report Cohens κ [12]. κ = 0 indicates the agreement expected by chance from the two sets of choices, and κ = 1 full agreement. In each pair, the image listed earlier in the sets file comes first. Counting both orders of every pair instead changes the median metrics κ by at most 0.04 on any set and no metrics κ by more than 0.11, and it leaves the ranking of metrics almost unchanged (Spearman correlation of at least 0.97). The best worst-case κ becomes 0.26 (Q-Align) instead of 0.23, so the absolute values depend somewhat on this convention. When both orders are counted, pairwise accuracy equals (κ+1)/2, so accuracy and this order-free κ rank metrics in the same way. Rankings between metrics are descriptive, and we do not test their differences for significance. Pairs that the metric scores as equal are excluded. This removes 20% to 22% of the pairs for VisualQuality-R1, the only metric that ties more than 5% of them, and 22% of the study pairs. In our study, the first image is always the raw photo. The 95% intervals resample scenes 1,000 times [46]. In our study, each vote is one pair, and the interval resamples raters and photos together. We do not use whole-set rank correlation, because it also rewards metric for distinguishing different photos, which no enhancement comparison requires. 3.4. Stress tests Simple edits. We apply six edits at moderate strength to the raw photo of each scene: CLAHE, red gain, Gaussian noise, saturation plus unsharp masking (S+S), S+S followed by CLAHE (S+S+C) and S+S plus noise (S+S+N). We use all 60 UID2021 scenes, all 100 SAUD scenes and 200 SOTA scenes, and count the scenes in which the edit scores above the enhancement with the highest opinion score. Gradient attack. For 5 differentiable metrics, we apply 10 PGD [36] steps of size ϵ/4 under an bound ϵ {2/255, 8/255} to the raw photo of the first 50 scenes of Figure 2. Agreement with people is low on every reference, and no metric performs well on all five. Within-scene κ (Sec. 3.3) of the eight metrics of Fig. 1, sorted by their worst value over the five references (last column). Blue: agreement, red: the metric prefers the image people liked less. Solid frame: the metrics own training set. Dashed frame: set from the same lab. Bottom rows: median and best value over all 73 metrics per reference (72 have all five values). The best values on UID2021 [20] and SAUD [23] come from metrics evaluated on their own training data. All metrics with their 95% intervals are listed in the appendix. the same three sets, save the result as an 8-bit PNG and rescore it. Since the photo is 8-bit and 255ϵ is an integer, rounding keeps the change within the bound. Generative drift. Following Banana100 [49], we send 20 UIEB photos (512 px) to Nano Banana Pro (gemini-3-proimage) and Nano Banana 2 (gemini-3.1-flash-image) [16, 17], feed each output back as the next input with fresh request, and keep the output size of the model. We score the chains with 72 of the metrics (all but LIQE-mix) and the patched MATLAB UCIQE code, 73 scores in total. The replica prompt is Banana100s Produce an exact replica of the provided image, with no alterations. (50 steps). The enhance prompt is Enhance this underwater photo: correct the colour cast and improve clarity and contrast, without changing its content. (20 steps). We measure noise with Immerkærs estimator [21] and color change as the mean CIE76 ab to step 1. As in Banana100, each score is min-max normalized, and score detects the drift when its mean change from step 1 is negative at every checkpoint (steps 5, 10 and 20, and 50 on the replica chains). Step 1, not the input, serves as the baseline, because the input has different size. 4. Agreement with human judgments 4.1. Agreement is low on all references No metric reaches κ = 0.41, the median agreement between two raters in our study, on all five references. This level comes from single raters on raw-versus-edit pairs, so for the opinion-score sets it is reference point rather than target. The best worst-case κ is 0.23 for Q-Align, followed by NR-UIQA at 0.22, with overlapping intervals  (Fig. 2)  . On our study alone, VisualQuality-R1 reaches 0.44, above the agreement between two raters, so the gap lies in consistency across references. This κ skips its ties. If tie counts as half correct choice, VisualQuality-R1 falls to rank 5 with accuracy 0.69, and LIQE is best with 0.72. Much of this agreement comes from which edits metric prefers. Choosing the peoples majority answer for each edit gives κ = 0.49, and replacing each metrics choices by its majority choice per edit changes the median κ from 0.21 to 0.22. With chance computed within each edit, two raters reach median κ of 0.13, LIQE 0.15 and Q-Align 0.12 (Tab. S2 in the appendix). The median metric reaches κ = 0.16 on UID2021, 0.25 on SAUD, 0.21 on SAUD2.0 [24], 0.10 on SOTA [54] and 0.21 in our study. High values occur only on single references: UIQAVSI reaches 0.92 on SAUD and QUIQ 0.70 on UID2021, both on their own training data. On SOTA, the largest set, 61 of 72 metrics remain below 0.2. The two standard underwater metrics are among the weakest. UCIQE [58] has κ 0.18 on UID2021 and 0.08, 0.21 and 0.17 on SAUD, SAUD2.0 and SOTA, where its entire 95% interval lies below zero on 3 sets. UIQM [41] ranges between 0.18 and 0.34 on the four opinion-score sets. Ranking methods. When methods are ranked by mean within-scene position, UCIQE orders the enhancement methods with Kendall τ of 0.23, 0.02, 0.18 and 0.24 against the human order on the four sets, negative on 3 of them. With 10 to 16 methods per set, these τ values indicate weak agreement rather than reversed order. UIQM gives 0.27 to 0.42. On UID2021, only 3 of 73 metrics identify the method people liked best. gMAD [35] and BAPPS-style 2AFC [64] results are in the appendix. 4.2. Generalization of learned underwater metrics Learned underwater metrics agree with people much more on their training set and same-lab data than elsewhere. The five learned metrics with known training set reach κ 0.60 to 0.92 on it, 0.58 to 0.65 on SAUD2.0 from the same lab, and at most 0.31 on data from other labs (Tab. 2). Shared photos do not explain this drop. Removing scenes whose photo also appears in the training set changes κ by at most 0.02. Small gradient steps succeed against every attacked metric With ϵ = 2/255, ten PGD steps raise the raw photo above the best human-rated enhancement in 100% of the 150 scenes for all 5 attacked metrics (Tab. 4), while the photo retains PSNR of at least 43.8 dB. Sensitivity to generative drift Under the strict rule of Banana100 [49], most metrics do not detect the drift. Every chain visibly changes the image (Fig. 1 and Fig. S1 of the appendix). Noise increases in 76 of 80 photo chains, mean noise σ rises by 1.4 to 2.8 from step 1 to the last step, and the color shifts by ab 24.7 to 51.2 (Tab. 5). The replica chains also turn the green cast red (mean becomes positive). These measures do not prove that people perceive worse image. On the enhance Figure 3. Agreement on individual pairs is the study κ (Tab. S7 in the appendix). Per-edit values are listed in the appendix. moderate CLAHE [71] or S+S+C edit may sometimes look better. Gaussian noise is not an enhancement, yet it outscores the best enhancement in up to 72% of scenes under UCIQE, 86% under FDUM and 74% under QUIQ [27]. People did not compare noise with the best enhancement either, but in our study they reject strong noise even against the raw photo. Only 8 metrics stay at or below half on every set and edit: NMFC, VisualQuality-R1, IL-NIQE, UIQM, Q-Align, LIQE, ARNIQA, NR-UIQA. 5.2. People reject edits that metrics reward Our study confirms that the edits metric rewards are not always the ones people prefer  (Fig. 3)  . People prefer mild CLAHE, contrast, sharpening and saturation, as well as moderate saturation, to the raw photo, and reject 7 of the 12 edits, 4 of them with the entire 95% interval below half (6 with equal weight per photo, see the appendix). On these 7 edits, UCIQE still prefers the edited photo in 91% of pairs, and UIQM [41] in 41%. After the saturate, sharpen and CLAHE chain is applied 20 times, 1% of votes prefer the result, whereas UCIQE prefers it for 100% of photos. Strong noise receives 9% of votes and 100% of UCIQEs choices. In contrast, Q-Align [55] and RALI [69] track people more closely and prefer few of the rejected edits. Figure 4. The Pro replica chain, which should change nothing yet becomes noisier, is therefore the clearest test. However, only 22, 11, 19 and 26 of 73 scores detect the drift on the Pro replica, NB2 replica, Pro enhance and NB2 enhance chains. Only 5 detect it on all four: ARNIQA-TID, MANIQA-PIPAL, NIMA-VGG16AVA, QualiCLIP+-SPAQ, RALI. Only RALI [69] among these is default checkpoint. This rule is strict. looser rule that checks only the last step credits 38 scores on the Pro replica chain and 24 on all four chains, including UIQM [41], Q-Align [55] and VisualQuality-R1 [57], but still not UCIQE [58]. UCIQE rises on all four chains, by +0.24, +0.36, +0.26 and +0.25 in normalized units, and decreases for at most 5% of photos on any chain. Among the hand-crafted underwater scores, only UIQM and UIConM detect any chain, and only the enhance chains. The visionlanguage scores decrease on average on every chain  (Fig. 4)  , but not at every checkpoint. Per photo, the best score decreases on 95% of Pro replica photos (ARNIQA-TID and RALI) but only on 65% of NB2 replica photos (ARNIQA-TID). UID2021 [20] SAUD [23] SAUD2.0 [24] SOTA [54] Study NaN share, MATLAB code as released κ, our NumPy port κ, MATLAB code, NaN patched 32% 0.18 0.34 38% 0.08 0.00 34% 0.21 0.15 27% 0.17 0.09 n/a 0.03 0. Table 6. Two UCIQE implementations give different answers. The public MATLAB code returns NaN for every image with pure-black pixel. With these NaNs replaced, its κ differs from that of our NumPy port by up to 0.16. 7. Causes of metric failure We examine three possible causes and label the untested parts as hypotheses. The UCIQE formula rewards the edits. UCIQE is weighted sum of the chroma spread, the luminance contrast and the mean saturation [58]. Saturation increases the first and third terms, unsharp masking and CLAHE [71] increase the second, and noise increases the first two. This is consistent with UCIQEs preference for S+S+C (Tab. 3), strong noise  (Fig. 3)  and the noisy, red-shifted drift frames (Tab. 5). We hypothesize that any score built from such global statistics, without model of how the scene should look, can be raised in this way. The public code does not always return score. The public MATLAB UCIQE code [42], run in GNU Octave [39], returns NaN whenever an image contains pureblack pixel, which occurs for 27% to 38% of the opinionscore images. Even on images for which both return score, our NumPy port and the MATLAB code rank images differently (Spearman correlation 0.48 to 0.79 per set). With the NaN patched, the two implementations differ in κ (Tab. 6), and the patched MATLAB UCIQE rises even more along the drift chains (+0.57 on Pro replica). Both versions divide chroma by L, which is unstable for near-black pixels. For example, 58% of the pixels in the last Pro replica frame of UIEB [29] photo 039 have < 1, which produces the ports value of 2.39 in Fig. 1. The qualitative UCIQE findings hold with the patched MATLAB code, although the magnitudes differ: S+S+C outscores the best enhancement in 35% to 90% of scenes (60% to 95% for our port), its κ in our study is 0.02, and it rises on all four drift chains, by +0.29 to +0.57. Only its κ on UID2021 [20] (0.34) is clearly higher than that of the port. Learned metrics change their choice under flips and resizing. Horizontally flipping both images of pair reverses metrics preference in median of 7% of withinscene pairs (up to 31%), and halving the image size does so in 27% (up to 47%), whereas UCIQE and UIQM [41], being global statistics, are unaffected by flips (the appendix). flip does not change quality. We hypothesize that part of the low agreement of learned metrics stems from this sensitivity rather than from an incorrect notion of quality. 8. Recommendations and conclusion Five recommendations. Our results suggest five checks for any paper that ranks underwater enhancement methods with an NR-IQA metric. (1) Report within-scene agreement with people on at least two references from different labs, and report the lower value. (2) Do not rank methods by UCIQE [58] alone, since its κ is near or below zero on three of the four opinion-score sets with either implementation (Tab. 6). (3) Include the raw photo and simple S+S+C edit as baselines. method that cannot outperform them under the chosen metric has not shown clear gain, and metric under which they often win should be checked against people before it is used to rank methods. (4) Report the implementation and version of every metric. (5) When the enhancement method is generative, measure noise and color change directly, because most metrics do not decrease as these grow. Limitations. Our study is small: 20 raters, all from our university, 32 photos and 12 edits, viewed on the raters own screens, and the raters agree with each other only moderately (median κ = 0.41). Blocks had 2, 3, 9 and 6 raters, so some photos have few votes. Pairs whose opinion scores differ by less than their rating noise are still counted, which can lower κ. Its references are raw UIEB [29] photos rather than enhancement outputs, and no person compared simple edit with the best enhancement or late drift frame with an early one. The drift test uses 20 photos, two editors and two prompts, and the outputs of the editors may change between model versions. Simple edits and attacks were applied to at most 200 and 50 scenes per set rather than to every scene, and the attacks target only 5 generalpurpose metrics, not the learned underwater metrics. We could not run every published underwater metric, and two learned metrics have training sets outside our references. The causes in Sec. 7 beyond UCIQEs formula and code are untested hypotheses. Societal impact. Underwater images support marine surveys and inspection, and metric that rewards noise or color shifts can promote enhancement methods that alter what scientist or inspector sees. We report our score manipulation tests so that evaluations can guard against them. All photos come from public research datasets used under their licenses. Raters agreed to take part on the study page before starting, could stop at any time by closing it, and were recorded without names: choices, response times, screen size, an age band and self-rated experience. is at code available https : Release. The //github.com/TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA and TrustUIQA at https://huggingface.co/datasets/ TrustUIQA/TrustUIQA, with the study choices, all scores and κ tables and the images we generated from UIEB photos. For the opinion-score sets and UIEB, which remain with their authors, we release image lists and scripts that rebuild our edits and attacks. Conclusion. Across 73 metrics and five human references, no metric reaches the median agreement between two of our raters on every reference. Learned underwater metrics agree with people mainly on data from their own lab, simple edits and small gradient steps outscore the enhancement people liked best, and few metrics detect the noise and color shifts of repeated generative edits. higher underwater quality score alone is not evidence of better image. Acknowledgments. We thank the 20 raters who took part in our study and the Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Society (AIMS) of Delhi Technological University.

Center crops (300 300 px) of UIEB photo 044, the first row block of Fig. 1, along the four chains. Every frame is resized to the Pro replica output size of this photo (1376 768 px) before cropping. The input is 512 px wide. The NB2 replica chain redraws the scene from step 10 on, so its later crops no longer match the input. This material provides the setup details and full tables behind the main paper. Every number is generated by scripts/make numbers.py from the result files. All metrics ran on one NVIDIA RTX 5070 Ti with 16 GB. The 2,800 Nano Banana images cost about US$285 at Googles list prices for the logged tokens. A. Edits, prompts and study details Images are in [0, 1]. Saturation multiplies Edit strengths. HSV saturation by 1.3, 1.6 or 2.0 (mild, moderate, strong). Unsharp masking adds a(xG2x) with Gaussian of σ = 2 and = 0.5, 1.5 or 3.0. CLAHE works on the channel with 8 8 tiles and clip limit 2, 4 or 8. Contrast scales the deviation from the image mean by 1.3, 1.6 or 2.0. Gaussian noise has standard deviation 0.02, 0.05 or 0.10. The red gain multiplies the red channel by 1.2, 1.5 or 2.0. The hue shift is 15, 45 or 90 degrees, and posterization keeps 5, 4 or 3 bits. One step of the S+S+C chain of our study applies saturation 1.15, unsharp masking with = 0.5 and CLAHE with clip limit 2. Generative editor prompts. Replica (Banana100s prompt): Produce an exact replica of the provided image, with no alterations. Enhance: Enhance this underwater photo: correct the colour cast and improve clarity and contrast, without changing its content. Every step is new request that contains only the prompt and the previous output. Figure S1 shows crops of one photo along the four chains.
